opus-5.5.text:
Thanks so much for having me. For us, artificial intelligence isn't really an add-on to bionic medicine. It's becoming the connective tissue between the person and the device.

The core challenge in our lab is this. When someone loses a limb, or loses function through injury or illness, we can build increasingly sophisticated robotic hardware. Modern prosthetic arms have many joints, wrists that rotate, hands that open and close in different grips. But the person has very few ways to tell that device what they want. They might have a couple of muscle signals in their residual limb, and suddenly they're trying to control something with far more degrees of freedom than they have control channels. So the bottleneck isn't the mechanics. It's the communication between the human and the machine.

That's where machine learning, and especially reinforcement learning, comes in for us. We think of the prosthesis not as a tool that waits for commands, but as a partner that learns over time. A device that can make predictions. It can anticipate what joint the person is likely to want to move next, what grip they'll need as they reach for a cup, or how their signals are changing as their muscles fatigue over the day. If the device can learn those predictions continually, while it's being used in the real world, it can start to fill in the gaps. It takes some of the burden off the person.

One of the ideas we've worked on a lot is what we call adaptive switching. Traditionally, an amputee might have to cycle through a fixed list of joints to choose which one to control, and that's slow and frustrating. If the system learns to predict which joint you're about to need and puts it at the top of the list, it saves a huge amount of time and cognitive effort. That's a small example, but it captures the bigger philosophy. The machine learns about the person and the person learns about the machine, and over time they build up a kind of shared understanding.

So I'd frame AI's role in our work as enabling a relationship rather than just a control scheme. We're interested in intelligent systems that learn continually, that build up predictive knowledge from their own ongoing experience, and that communicate back to the person, maybe through sensory feedback, so the loop goes both ways. Ultimately, the goal is for the device to feel less like an external machine you operate and more like an extension of yourself, something that's genuinely part of the body and part of how you move through the world.

r002.rationale: It describes AI learning from a person’s signals and predicting the joints or grips they intend to use, helping translate their intent into prosthetic action.

r003.rationale: It identifies prostheses as an application of reinforcement learning, but does not describe wearable prosthetic limbs operating in very low-compute environments.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, artificial intelligence in our lab is really about communication. When someone loses a limb and we fit them with a bionic arm, the hard problem isn't the hardware anymore. We can build hands with many motors and many degrees of freedom. The hard problem is that the person has very few channels left to tell that device what they want it to do. They might have two or three muscle signals they can control, and we're asking them to drive a device with a dozen different motions.

So the device needs to meet them halfway. That's where machine learning, and specifically reinforcement learning, comes in. We want the prosthesis to learn from its ongoing interaction with the person: what they tend to do next, how they move, what grips they use in what situations. Over time it builds up predictions, a kind of running understanding of its user, and it can use those predictions to anticipate and reduce the burden on the person. Instead of the person controlling every joint one at a time, the arm starts to do some of the work of knowing what comes next.

What I find most exciting is that this is a very natural setting for the ideas coming out of reinforcement learning more broadly. The device is an agent. It's embedded in the world, it's getting a continuous stream of experience, and it has to learn in real time from a single person over a long period. There's no giant dataset to pretrain on, because every person is different and every person changes. So the learning has to happen on the device, in the moment, in a way that's safe and understandable to the user.

And I'd say the goal isn't to replace the person's intent. It's to make the technology feel less like a tool you have to fight with and more like a partner. The best outcome is when someone stops thinking about the arm altogether and just gets on with their life.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using a few remaining muscle signals to control the prosthesis, but does not describe rewiring the human nervous system.

r002.rationale: It frames AI as helping bridge the gap between a person’s limited control signals and the prosthesis’s many motions, learning the user’s likely intentions to anticipate actions and reduce control effort.

r003.rationale: It identifies prostheses as an application of reinforcement learning and says learning occurs on-device in real time, but does not characterize the setting as very low-compute.

astra-6.text:
I see artificial intelligence as a way to make bionic devices active partners in a person’s life. A prosthetic limb is a good example: it’s not just a question of building better motors or sensors. It’s also a question of how the person and the device learn to work together.

The person is learning how to use the limb, and we’d like the limb to learn about the person—their signals, their preferences, and what they’re trying to accomplish. AI gives us tools for that ongoing adaptation. Rather than putting the entire burden of learning on the person, we can have the technology share some of that burden.

The goal is to make a device more useful in everyday life: something that responds in a way that feels natural and helps someone do what matters to them.

r002.rationale: It says AI helps a limb learn a person's signals, preferences, and goals, but does not clearly describe AI as translating intentions into what the limb can deliver.

sol-6.1.text:
In our lab, we see artificial intelligence as a way to make bionic devices active partners in a person’s life. A prosthetic arm, for example, shouldn’t simply wait for commands. It should be able to learn from its interactions with the person using it, anticipate what might be useful, and adapt as that person’s needs change.

That makes the problem less about building a clever controller in isolation and more about how a person and a machine learn together. The person is learning to use the device, and the device can also be learning about the person. We’re interested in how that ongoing interaction can make the technology more intuitive and useful.

Ultimately, the measure of success is what someone can do with it in their everyday life. AI is a means to support that person’s agency and abilities.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adapting a prosthetic through interaction, but it does not describe rewiring the human nervous system.

r002.rationale: It says the device can learn about and anticipate the person, but does not present AI as translating the person’s intentions into what the limb can deliver.

r003.rationale: It mentions a prosthetic arm but does not identify reinforcement learning or very low-compute environments.
